title: Quantum and Cryptographic Resilience for Firms
summary: An eight-module programme helping firms understand the quantum threat, build a cryptographic inventory, plan post-quantum migration and report readiness to the board and supervisors.
intro: This training programme equips firms to prepare for quantum computing: understanding the threat to today's cryptography, building a cryptographic inventory, planning post-quantum migration with vendors and infrastructures, and reporting progress to the board and supervisors.

sections.Aim and Purpose: To give technology, security, risk and business leaders a practical, non-mathematical grounding in the quantum threat and what it means for their firm's systems, data and third parties. Participants leave able to scope a cryptographic inventory, prioritise exposure, plan a credible multi-year migration and report quantum readiness to the board and the authority.
sections.What It Covers: Quantum computing and the cryptographic threat, harvest now decrypt later, where cryptography sits in the firm, building a cryptographic inventory, risk assessment and prioritisation, NIST post-quantum standards and crypto-agility, migration planning and delivery, vendors, payment and market infrastructures and digital assets, and governance, board reporting and supervisory engagement.
Intended Audience: Chief information security officers, chief technology officers, architects and security engineering leads
Operational resilience, technology risk, third-party risk and internal audit staff
Senior managers and programme sponsors accountable for cyber, data protection and change
Learning Objectives: Explain in plain language why quantum computing threatens public-key cryptography and why the firm should act now
Identify where cryptography sits across the firm's systems, data, products and third parties
Build a cryptographic inventory and prioritise systems by exposure, data shelf life and criticality
Plan a credible, crypto-agile migration to the NIST post-quantum standards
Manage dependencies on vendors, payment schemes, market infrastructures and digital asset networks
Govern the programme and report quantum readiness to the board and supervisors
sections.Structure and Format: Eight modules of about three hours each, delivered in person, virtually or in a hybrid format, either as a four-day programme or as a series of half-day sessions. Each module combines a briefing with case studies and practical exercises using inventory and roadmap templates, and modules can be selected or tailored to the firm's technology estate.
sections.Useful Prior Knowledge and Experience: Some experience of information security, technology risk or operational resilience is helpful. No knowledge of quantum physics or cryptographic mathematics is required.
Core Reading: NIST, FIPS 203, 204 and 205: Post-Quantum Cryptography Standards (2024)
G7 Cyber Expert Group, Public Statement on Planning for the Opportunities and Risks of Quantum Computing (2024)
FSB, Enhancing Third-Party Risk Management and Oversight: A Toolkit for Financial Institutions and Financial Authorities (2023)

modules.title: Quantum Computing and the Cryptographic Threat
modules.summary: A plain-language introduction to quantum computing, why it breaks today's public-key cryptography, the uncertainty around timelines and why data harvested now may be decrypted later.
objectives: Explain in plain language how quantum computers differ from classical computers
Distinguish the impact of quantum attacks on public-key and symmetric cryptography
Assess the harvest now, decrypt later risk and its link to data shelf life
syllabus: Qubits, error correction and the path to cryptographically relevant machines
Why public-key encryption and digital signatures are most at risk
Timeline estimates and why uncertainty is not a reason to wait
Harvest now, decrypt later and long-lived confidential data

modules.title: Where Cryptography Sits in Your Firm
modules.summary: A map of where cryptography protects a financial services firm, from client channels and trading links to payment messaging, hardware security modules, certificates and signatures on ledgers.
objectives: Identify the main uses of cryptography in the firm's business services
Recognise cryptography embedded in legacy, cloud and vendor systems
Link cryptographic dependencies to important business services and client data
syllabus: Secure communications, certificates and public key infrastructure
Client portals, trading connectivity and payment messaging
Hardware security modules, key management and digital signatures
Cryptography hidden in vendor products, libraries and cloud services

modules.title: Building the Cryptographic Inventory
modules.summary: How to discover and record where and how cryptography is used across the firm and its supply chain, who owns the inventory and how to keep it complete and decision-useful.
objectives: Design the scope, data fields and ownership of a cryptographic inventory
Combine discovery tools, architecture review and vendor information
Test the inventory for completeness, including third-party and embedded uses
syllabus: Discovery tools, manual review and the cryptographic bill of materials
Data fields: algorithm, key length, location, owner and dependency
Gathering information from vendors and outsourced providers
Common gaps: partial scope, no named owner and stale records

modules.title: Risk Assessment and Prioritisation
modules.summary: How to turn the inventory into a risk-based view of quantum exposure, ranking systems by data sensitivity and shelf life, business criticality and difficulty of change, within the firm's risk appetite.
objectives: Assess quantum exposure using data shelf life, sensitivity and system criticality
Prioritise remediation by risk and by time and effort to migrate
Integrate quantum risk into the firm's cyber, technology and operational risk frameworks
syllabus: Exposure scoring: data shelf life, migration time and threat timeline
Linking to important business services and impact tolerances
Risk appetite, risk register entries and key risk indicators
Case study: prioritising a firm's systems for migration

modules.title: Post-Quantum Standards and Crypto-Agility
modules.summary: The NIST post-quantum standards, how hybrid approaches work during transition, and why designing for crypto-agility matters as much as choosing the right algorithm.
objectives: Explain the NIST post-quantum standards and their intended uses
Evaluate hybrid deployment, performance impacts and interoperability
Apply crypto-agility as a design principle in architecture and procurement
syllabus: NIST post-quantum standards: ML-KEM, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA
Hybrid schemes during transition and their trade-offs
Performance, key sizes and interoperability testing
Crypto-agility in architecture, coding standards and procurement

modules.title: Planning and Running the Migration Programme
modules.summary: What a realistic multi-year migration programme involves, from roadmap and resourcing to testing, sequencing and integration with the firm's wider technology change and refresh cycles.
objectives: Design a migration roadmap with milestones, dependencies and resourcing
Sequence migration to protect high-value data and critical services first
Manage testing, change control and rollback for cryptographic change
syllabus: Roadmaps, milestones and alignment with technology refresh cycles
Business case, budget and skills for a multi-year programme
Testing, change management and rollback
Measuring progress: coverage, exceptions and residual risk

modules.title: Vendors, Infrastructures and Digital Assets
modules.summary: Why most firms depend on vendors, cloud providers, payment schemes and market infrastructures to migrate, and the particular quantum challenges for blockchains, wallets and digital asset custody.
objectives: Assess vendor and cloud provider post-quantum roadmaps and contractual commitments
Coordinate migration with payment schemes, market infrastructures and counterparties
Evaluate quantum risks to blockchain signatures, wallets and custody of digital assets
syllabus: Vendor due diligence, contract clauses and supply chain assurance
Coordinated migration across payment and settlement systems
Exposed public keys, wallet design and blockchain upgrade risk
Implications for crypto-asset custody and tokenised assets

modules.title: Governance, Board Reporting and Supervisory Engagement
modules.summary: Brings the programme together into a governance and reporting model for quantum readiness: accountability, board information, assurance and the evidence the firm should be able to show the authority.
objectives: Allocate accountability for quantum readiness across the three lines of defence
Specify the management information and assurance the board needs
Prepare the evidence of quantum readiness that supervisors will expect
syllabus: Ownership, steering groups and the role of internal audit
Board reporting: inventory coverage, milestones, exceptions and dependencies
International work: BIS, G7 Cyber Expert Group and national cyber agencies
Workshop: the firm's quantum readiness plan and board paper
